final_answer: Culture lacks serum corona, liver HARE clearance, hyaluronidase-rich blood/tissue, and flow; in vivo these strip or clear the particles before tumor accumulation - the standard translation gap for HA carriers.
note: Evidence is off-topic: windows cover cell-culture/HARE transfection methods and liver-fibrosis serum markers; nothing states serum corona, liver HARE clearance of nanoparticles, hyaluronidase-rich blood/tissue, or flow stripping/clearing particles before tumor accumulation.

final_answer: Intra-articular injection of HA preparations into a joint (classically the osteoarthritic knee) to restore synovial-fluid viscoelasticity and lubrication.
note: Evidence PMC3617354 states IA HA injection aims at decreasing OA-related pain and improving joint function by restoring synovial fluid physiological properties, and that high synovial fluid viscoelasticity is necessary for lubrication.

final_answer: BDDE (1,4-butanediol diglycidyl ether).
note: Evidence PMC4264939 states 1,4-butanediol diglycidyl ether (BDDE) 'is the crosslinking agent used in the majority of the market-leading HA fillers' and is the industry standard.

final_answer: About 15 g total, with roughly one-third degraded and replaced daily - among the fastest turnover rates of any body component.
note: Evidence PMC8561002 states 'one-third of total body HA (~15 g in a person with a 70 kg body weight) is turned over daily' and calls this an extremely rapid turnover versus months/years for other ECM molecules.

final_answer: By injecting hyaluronidase to enzymatically dissolve the HA filler.
note: Evidence PMC11217013 states hyaluronidase is particularly useful where vascular complications have occurred due to intravascular HA filler injection; PMC9340193 states the HA filler can be degraded by hyaluronidase when vascular complications develop.

final_answer: Its high viscoelasticity maintains anterior-chamber depth and protects the corneal endothelium during phacoemulsification and lens implantation.
note: Evidence PMC2684437 states OVDs are used to maintain the anterior chamber and coat the endothelium during cataract surgery; PMC3107822 states OVDs maintain adequate intraocular space and decrease possible damage of the corneal endothelium in phacoemulsification.

final_answer: Roughly 0.5 to >6 MDa across preparations (MW 500 kDa to >6,000 kDa).
note: Draft's standard-preparation 0.5-3 MDa subrange and hylan G-F 20 average of ~6 MDa are not in the evidence; the decisive fragment is: "MW (500 kDa to >6,000 kDa)" (PMC8808930).

final_answer: About 20 mg/mL (most brands fall in the 17.5-24 mg/mL range).
note: No evidence window gives any HA concentration (mg/mL) for crosslinked dermal fillers; windows discuss filler composition, crosslinking and residence-time modeling only, so the 20 mg/mL figure and 17.5-24 mg/mL range cannot be verified from this pack.

final_answer: Native, uncrosslinked HA has a half-life of a few days in human tissues, and chemical crosslinking (most commonly with BDDE) is used to increase filler lifetime in the body.
note: Draft's under-24-hour skin half-life, sub-day synovial residence and 6-24 month filler duration are not in the evidence; the decisive fragment is: "As it has a few days of half-life in human tissues, HA-based dermal filler is chemically modified to increase its lifetime in the body" (PMC6197218).

final_answer: Endre (Endel) Balazs, who also developed the first HA-based biomedical products (e.g., Healon for eye surgery).
note: No evidence window mentions Endre Balazs, coinage of the term 'viscosupplementation', or development of the first HA biomedical products; windows are off-topic (glaucoma eye drops, dry eye) apart from noting Stegman's 1978 Healon injection.

final_answer: About 6-7 MDa (several million Da), falling in osteoarthritis.
note: Evidence only lists MW ranges analyzed in synovial fluid (2.5-7 MDa, 1-2.5 MDa, 0.5-1 MDa, 0.03-0.5 MDa) and an age-associated decrease in HA concentration; it does not state an approximate healthy MW of 6-7 MDa or that MW falls in osteoarthritis.

final_answer: About 10 mg/mL (1%) sodium hyaluronate of high MW (~4 MDa).
note: Draft's ~4-5 MDa upper figure is not in the evidence; the decisive fragment is: "Healon (sodium hyaluronate 1%, 4 x 10^6 daltons)" (PMC2698691).

final_answer: Severe acute inflammatory joint reactions (pseudosepsis): severe inflammation of the joint, often with significant effusion and significant pain, occurring after more than one injection and with infection ruled out; such reactions have been reported after intra-articular HA injections, including avian-derived hylan G-F 20.
note: Draft's 'mainly with' hylan claim and conservative/re-injection management are not settled by the evidence (reports are conflicting and the avian allergic-type role was not supported); the decisive fragment is: "they defined pseudosepsis as having certain characteristics, which include severe inflammation of the joint, often with significant polymorphonuclear cellular effusion and significant pain" (PMC8808807).

final_answer: A bioresorbable membrane composed of chemically modified sodium hyaluronate (HA) and carboxymethylcellulose (CMC), placed at surgery as an adhesion barrier to reduce the incidence, extent, and severity of postoperative adhesions.
note: Draft's gelling-on-contact and resorption-within-about-a-week details are not in the evidence; the decisive fragment is: "Seprafilm adhesion barrier is a bioresorbable membrane composed of chemically modified sodium hyaluronate (HA) and carboxymethylcellulose (CMC)" (PMC3401301).

final_answer: Cohesive OVDs contain high-molecular-weight HA and protect intraocular tissues by maintaining a deep anterior chamber due to their high viscoelasticity; dispersive OVDs tend to adhere to tissue, resulting in greater corneal endothelial protection during phacoemulsification.
note: Draft's hold-together/removed-as-a-mass and lower-MW/harder-to-remove claims are not in the evidence; the decisive fragment is: "Cohesive OVDs containing high molecular weight HA protect intraocular tissues ... by maintaining a deep anterior chamber due to their high viscoelasticity" and dispersive OVDs "tend to adhere to tissue, resulting in greater corneal endothelial protection" (PMC12048296).

final_answer: To replenish the bladder's protective glycosaminoglycan (GAG) layer, whose depletion makes the epithelium leaky and exposes the bladder wall to urine solutes and irritants; HA (often instilled with chondroitin sulfate) reduces bladder pain, urgency, and frequency.
note: Draft's claim that HA can raise bladder capacity is not in the evidence; the decisive fragment is: "the GAG deficiency results in a 'leaky' epithelium, allowing the passage and influx of potassium ions, bacteria, and urine solutes towards the bladder tissue" (PMC11013000), and instillations of chondroitin and hyaluronic acid improved bladder pain, urgency, and frequency.

final_answer: HA dressings maintain a moist healing environment and actively modulate the wound: fragment signaling recruits cells early, and HA supports re-epithelialization and ECM remodeling.
note: Evidence supports only generic dressing properties (moist environment, improved granulation and re-epithelialization for interactive dressings generally); no window states HA fragment signaling recruits cells early or that HA supports ECM remodeling, so the HA-specific rationale beyond moisture is not settled by this pack.

final_answer: B - ophthalmic (cataract) surgery, as a viscoelastic protecting the corneal endothelium.
note: Evidence PMC6393256 states that since the introduction of HEALON OVD (sodium hyaluronate 1%) the safety and outcome of cataract surgery has vastly improved, and that HEALON products were used for protection of endothelial cells - matching option B.

final_answer: Their primary action is physical (space filling and water binding) rather than pharmacological/metabolic, so they are regulated as implantable devices (e.g., FDA Class III devices).
note: Evidence PMC13230627 states dermal fillers maintain volume 'through a physical restorative effect rather than pharmacological action'; PMC4948701 states HA injections are classified by the FDA as class III medical devices based on a mechanical/viscoelastic rather than biological mechanism of action.

final_answer: It forms a protective, hydrating film over ulcerated mucosa and supports re-epithelialization, reducing pain from chemotherapy/radiation-induced mucositis.
note: No evidence window mentions a protective/hydrating film over ulcerated mucosa or re-epithelialization; windows describe a combined vitamin E/triamcinolone/HA mouthwash, HA reducing ROS effects and improving healing, and pain as an outcome measure, which does not settle the draft's HA-specific film mechanism.
